summary: Ahmose I expelled the Hyksos and reunited Egypt (c. 1549–1524 BCE); his successors, above all Thutmose III, built an empire from Nubia beyond the Fourth Cataract to the Euphrates. Egypt contested Syria with Mitanni and then the Hittites until the treaty of c. 1259 BCE, but after Ramesses III fought off the Sea Peoples its power ebbed, and by Ramesses XI's death in 1077 BCE the country was split between Tanis and Thebes. Reign dates follow the conventional low chronology and are approximate.
details: For about a century the Hyksos, kings of Near Eastern origin, had ruled northern Egypt from Avaris in the Delta, while a native dynasty held Thebes in the south. Ahmose's father, Seqenenre Tao, probably died fighting them, and his brother Kamose raided the lands around Avaris before dying after a short reign. Ahmose came to the throne as a boy of about ten, so the war paused under a regency. His reign, conventionally dated c. 1549–1524 BCE, would finish the struggle and is counted as the start of the Eighteenth Dynasty and the New Kingdom.

Once grown, Ahmose moved down the eastern Delta and seized the border fortress of Tjaru, cutting Avaris off from help in Canaan. According to the tomb inscription of a soldier, Ahmose son of Ebana, the king attacked Avaris several times and took it on the fourth attempt, probably by his 18th or 19th regnal year. He then besieged the Hyksos stronghold of Sharuhen near Gaza for three years. With the Hyksos gone, Upper and Lower Egypt were one kingdom again, ruled from Thebes, and Egyptian armies stood on the edge of Canaan.

Thutmose I, a military man who came to power through marriage into the royal family, set out to push Egypt's borders further than ever. In Nubia he built a fortress at Tombos near the Third Cataract, and an inscription of his has been found at Kurgus, beyond the Fourth Cataract. In the Levant he marched to the Euphrates, becoming the first pharaoh to cross it, and set up a victory stele there. The Syrian princes stopped paying tribute after he left, but his campaigns marked out the frontiers, from Nubia to the Euphrates, that later kings tried to hold.

When Thutmose II died, his heir Thutmose III was a small child (estimates of his age range from two to 13). His stepmother and aunt Hatshepsut, Thutmose II's widow and a daughter of Thutmose I, acted as regent. By about the seventh year of the reign she had taken the full titles of a pharaoh and ruled as senior co-king, with Thutmose III as junior partner. Her roughly 20-year rule was mostly peaceful and prosperous, with major building at Karnak and trading expeditions. Thutmose III became sole ruler only at her death, c. 1458 BCE.

Soon after Hatshepsut died, the king of Kadesh led a coalition of Canaanite and Syrian rulers that gathered at Megiddo, a fortress controlling the main route north. Thutmose III marched from Egypt and, against his generals' advice, took his army through the narrow Aruna pass, surprising the enemy and routing them. The survivors fled into Megiddo, which surrendered after a siege of about seven months. The battle is usually dated 1457 BCE, though some place it in 1482 or 1479. Taking Megiddo gave Egypt control of northern Canaan and forced the Syrian princes to send tribute and hostages.

Mitanni, a Hurrian kingdom in northern Syria and Mesopotamia, was Egypt's main rival for Syria. In his 33rd year (c. 1447 BCE), on his eighth campaign, Thutmose III had boats built at Byblos and carried them overland through Syria, past Aleppo and Carchemish. He crossed the Euphrates, catching the Mitannian king unprepared, pillaged towns on the far bank, and set up a stele beside the one left by his grandfather Thutmose I. The raid did not conquer Mitanni, but it showed Egypt's reach and brought gifts from distant kings, which Thutmose recorded as tribute.

Egypt's southern empire in Nubia (Kush) supplied gold, ivory, ebony, cattle and soldiers, and was run by a viceroy. In his 50th year, about 1430 BCE, the aging Thutmose III led his last campaign, a march into Nubia as far as the Fourth Cataract of the Nile. No Egyptian king had taken an army so far south before, although Egyptian influence already reached the area around Gebel Barkal. By the end of his reign Egypt directly controlled the Nile valley up to the Fourth Cataract, its greatest southern extent.

Amenhotep IV came to the throne c. 1353 or 1351 BCE and in his fifth year renamed himself Akhenaten, 'beneficial to the Aten', the sun disc. He turned away from Amun and the traditional gods and founded a new capital, Akhetaten (modern Amarna), in Middle Egypt. The Amarna letters found there show his vassals in Syria and Canaan pleading for help as the Hittites under Suppiluliuma I replaced Mitanni as the great northern power. Egypt lost the province of Amurru when its ruler went over to the Hittites. After Akhenaten's death the old religion returned and Amarna was abandoned.

Horemheb, a general who became the last king of the Eighteenth Dynasty, had no surviving children. He chose as heir his vizier Paramessu, an army officer from a military family in the Delta, who had a son, Seti, and a grandson to secure the succession. Paramessu took the throne as Ramesses I. His reign lasted only a year or two (often dated 1292–1290 BCE, though 1295–1294 is also cited), but he founded the Nineteenth Dynasty, whose kings Seti I and Ramesses II set out to win back Egypt's lost lands in Syria.

Seti I had briefly recaptured Kadesh and Amurru, but both seem to have slipped back under Hittite control. In his fifth year, generally dated May 1274 BCE, Ramesses II marched north to retake them and met the Hittite king Muwatalli II near Kadesh on the Orontes River. With perhaps 5,000 to 6,000 chariots in all, it may be the largest chariot battle ever fought. Ramesses was ambushed and surrounded, then rallied his troops and drove the Hittites back. The battle ended in stalemate, but Muwatalli kept Kadesh and pushed into Egyptian territory, leaving Egypt's Asian empire limited to Canaan.

After Kadesh the fighting dragged on for years, while Egypt worried about the Sea Peoples and the Hittites about rising Assyria. Around 1259 BCE (some accounts give 1258, Ramesses II's 21st year), Ramesses and the Hittite king Hattusili III agreed what is the oldest surviving peace treaty. Both sides promised not to invade each other, to hand back political refugees, and to help each other against enemies. The treaty fixed the Syrian frontier where it stood, with Egypt keeping Canaan and the Hittites holding Kadesh and Amurru, and it kept the peace until the Hittite Empire collapsed decades later.

Around 1200 BCE the Late Bronze Age world was falling apart, and groups that scholars call the Sea Peoples, among them the Peleset (Philistines) and Shardana, attacked the eastern Mediterranean. In his eighth year Ramesses III met them twice: on land at Djahy, on Egypt's frontier in the Levant, and in the Nile Delta, where his fleet ambushed their ships while archers lined the banks. Egypt survived when the Hittite Empire and many other states did not. But the cost was high, and the Philistines settled in southern Canaan as Egypt's hold on Asia faded.

In the 20th Dynasty Egypt was hit by poor Nile floods, famine, unrest and corruption, and the loss of its empire in Asia. Under Ramesses XI, royal power weakened so far that the High Priests of Amun at Thebes became the real rulers of Upper Egypt, while Smendes controlled the north. When Ramesses XI died in 1077 BCE, Smendes buried him and founded the 21st Dynasty at Tanis in the Delta. The New Kingdom was over: Egypt entered the Third Intermediate Period, divided between Tanis and Thebes, with its foreign empire gone.
